newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FORECAST-Swedish Riksbank to cut repo rate nxt wk.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Swedish Riksbank to cut repo rate nxt wk.

text.p: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, was expected to cut its key interest rate, the repo, by between 15 and 25 basis points next week, most likely at its weekly tender on Tuesday, a Reuters poll found on Friday.
Of 13 analysts surveyed, 10 were expecting a lowering of the repo rate, which was last cut to 4.10 percent on December 17.
"We think that the Riksbank will lower by between 20 and 25 basis points presumably on Tuesday," economist Deborah Bennelick from UBS told Reuters.

She said the positive outlook for inflation, the strength of the crown and lower interest rates overseas all combined to support a further cut to the repo rate, which has been trimmed from 8.91 percent at the start of 1996.
Two of the economists questioned forecast a cut of 15 basis points, two a cut of between 15 and 20, three between 20-25 basis points and three expected a 25 basis point lowering.
The optimism over the repo rate was due largely to the outlook for continuing low inflation.

The market believed that the consumer price index for December, due to be released at 0815 GMT on January 21, just 15 minutes before the reverse repurchase operation, would show continuing negative inflation trends.
One analyst forecast the Riksbank would lower the repo next week but not necessarily on Tuesday.

"The lowering will come next week but not necessarily on Tuesday. They are awaiting more CPI and retail sales data in order to eventually lower both the repo rate and the interest rate corridor on Thursday (at a Riksbank board meeting)," he said.
The deposit and lending rates, marking out the floor and ceiling of the rate corridor, currently stand at 3.75 percent and 5.25 percent.
Three of the 13 economist did not think the Riksbank would lower the repo rate next Tuesday.

"They will barely have time to analyse the consumer price index figures before announcing the repo rate. Furthermore important information from the SCB (Sweden's central statistics bureau) on retail sales and industrial production are expected the day after," said one analyst.
But the market had already factored in a repo rate cut and a negative effect on the debt market was expected if the cut did not come through.
"The market has discounted a lowering and there are many people who will be disappointed if the Riksbank does not move on Tuesday," said one analyst.
According to a Reuters forecast for January, economists on average expected the repo rate to bottom at 3.53 percent in the first half of 1997.

Economists interviewed for the poll were from Aragon, Carnegie, Consensus, Den Danske Bank, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, Hagstrmer & Qviberg, Handelsbanken, JP Morgan, Merrill, Nomura, S-E-Banken, Swedbank, and UBS.
